title: TypeScript and Node.js
description: How TypeScript's types catch mistakes before code runs, and how Node.js runs JavaScript outside the browser, ending with a small typed service that validates what enters it.
audience: A capable adult who can read JavaScript (the language lessons of the-web-html-css-javascript, or equivalent) and has used a command line.
outcomes: You'll be able to predict the type TypeScript infers and read its error messages.
You'll be able to narrow unions, write generics and derive types from other types.
You'll be able to predict the order of callbacks in Node and what blocks the event loop.
You'll be able to read an HTTP handler, a stream and a semver range, and design a service that validates its input.

modules.title: The type system
modules.summary: What types are, how TypeScript infers and narrows them, and how generics and type operators describe code you have not written yet.

modules.title: The Node.js runtime
modules.summary: How Node runs JavaScript outside the browser: modules, the event loop, bytes and streams, HTTP and failure handling.

modules.title: Building services
modules.summary: Packages, versions and tests, and a typed service that validates what enters it and shuts down cleanly.

lessons.title: What types are for
lessons.objective: Explain that types exist only at compile time, read a basic compiler error and say what the compiled JavaScript contains.

concepts.title: Static type
concepts.summary: A label the compiler attaches to a value or expression to check how it is used before the program runs.

concepts.title: Type erasure
concepts.summary: Annotations, interfaces and type aliases are removed when TypeScript is compiled, so none of them exist at run time.

concepts.title: Compile time and run time
concepts.summary: The checker reports mistakes before running, but by default the compiler still emits JavaScript when it finds errors.

concepts.title: The compiler
concepts.summary: tsc reads TypeScript and tsconfig.json, checks types, and writes JavaScript for the chosen target.

misconceptions: Learners think the types still exist when the program runs. They are erased, so typeof or instanceof can never check an interface.
Learners think a type error stops the build. By default tsc reports the error and still writes the JavaScript, unless noEmitOnError is set.
Learners think a typed value is validated. Types describe what the author promises, and nothing checks data from outside.
sequence: Show let n: number = 5; n = "five" and read the message and code.
Compile const x: number = 1; interface A { a: number } and show the JavaScript, which contains only const x = 1;.
Run a file with an error and show that JavaScript is still written.
Name the three jobs: catch mistakes, document intent, enable editor tooling.
examples: let n: number = 5; n = "five"; reports error TS2322: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'. (TypeScript 5.6).
const x: number = 1; interface A { a: number } type T = string; function f(a: number): string { return String(a) } compiles to const x = 1; and function f(a) { return String(a); }.
tsc exits with a non-zero code on that error but still writes the .js file.

figures.shows: A pipeline: .ts source, type checker (error list), type eraser, .js output. Views: the file with its annotations highlighted, then the same file with them removed.
figures.learnerAction: Toggle between source and output to see which tokens vanish.

figures.shows: Six snippets of TypeScript, each with a choice of which parts remain in the JavaScript.
figures.learnerAction: Pick the surviving text.

questionPlan.answer: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'.
choices: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'.
Expected a string but received a number.

questionPlan.sample:
Compile with tsc: const x: number = 1; interface A { a: number }
What is the entire JavaScript output?

Reports the error and writes nothing.

lessons.title: Inference and literal types
lessons.objective: Predict the type TypeScript infers for a declaration, including how let, const and as const change it.

concepts.title: Type inference
concepts.summary: The compiler works out a type from the initial value, so annotations are needed mainly at boundaries.

concepts.title: Widening
concepts.summary: A mutable location widens a literal to its general type, so let a = 5 is number while const b = 5 has the literal type 5.

concepts.title: as const
concepts.summary: as const freezes a literal expression to its narrowest, readonly type.

concepts.title: Arrays and tuples
concepts.summary: [1, 'a'] is an array of string or number, and [string, number] is a tuple of fixed length and position types.

misconceptions: Learners think const and let infer the same type. const keeps the literal type, so const b = 5 has type 5.
Learners annotate everything. Inference already gives the right type in most places.
Learners think an object literal's string property has a literal type. It is widened to string unless as const is used.
sequence: Infer types for let a = 5, const b = 5 and let c = [1, 'a'].
Show const d = { kind: 'circle' } as { kind: string } and the same with as const as { readonly kind: 'circle' }.
Tuple: const t: [string, number] = ['a', 1, 2] fails on length.
Where to annotate: function parameters, exported functions and empty collections.
examples: let a = 5 has type number; const b = 5 has type 5; let c = [1, "a"] has type (string | number)[].
const d = { kind: "circle" } has type { kind: string }; with as const it is { readonly kind: "circle" }.
const dirs = ["up", "down"] as const gives readonly ["up", "down"], and typeof dirs[number] is "up" | "down".

figures.shows: Rows of declarations with columns for what the checker infers, hidden until the learner chooses, using declarations different from the questions.
figures.learnerAction: Predict each type then reveal.

figures.shows: A type lattice from literal 5 up to number up to unknown, with an arrow showing widening at let and not at const.
figures.learnerAction: Pick let or const and watch the arrow.

questionPlan.sample:
const b = 5;
What is the type of b? Give it as TypeScript prints it.

let c = [1, "a"];
What type does TypeScript infer for c?

const e = { kind: "circle" } as const;
What is the type of e?

lessons.title: Shapes and structural typing
lessons.objective: Decide whether a value fits an object type by its shape, and predict when excess property checks and readonly stop an assignment.

concepts.title: Object type
concepts.summary: An object type lists property names, their types and whether each is optional or readonly.

concepts.title: Structural typing
concepts.summary: A value fits a type when it has at least the required properties with compatible types, whatever it was declared as.

concepts.title: Excess property check
concepts.summary: A fresh object literal assigned to a type may not name properties the type lacks, though a variable holding the same object may.

concepts.title: Interface and type alias
concepts.summary: Both describe shapes; interfaces can be extended and merged, and aliases can name unions and other non-object types.

misconceptions: Learners think a class instance must be declared as an interface's implementer to fit it. Shape alone decides.
Learners think the excess property error means the extra property is wrong at run time. It is a typo guard on fresh literals only.
Learners think readonly protects data at run time. It is erased, and only the checker enforces it.
sequence: A class Dog with a name property assigned to an interface Named, with no declared relationship.
A literal { x: 1, y: 2 } assigned straight to { x: number } fails, but assigning a variable that holds it passes.
readonly x on an interface and the assignment p.x = 2.
Optional properties and the undefined they add.
examples: interface Named { name: string } class Dog { name = "d"; bark(){} } const n: Named = new Dog(); compiles with no error.
const p: { x: number } = { x: 1, y: 2 } reports TS2353; const q = { x: 1, y: 2 }; const p2: { x: number } = q; has no error.
interface P { readonly x: number } const p: P = { x: 1 }; p.x = 2; reports TS2540: Cannot assign to 'x' because it is a read-only property.

Rejects it, because Dog has an extra bark method.

const p: { x: number } = { x: 1, y: 2 };

lessons.title: Unions and narrowing
lessons.objective: Narrow a union with typeof, in, equality and discriminant checks, and use never to prove a switch is exhaustive.

concepts.title: Union type
concepts.summary: A | B allows either type, and only operations valid for both are allowed until the value is narrowed.

concepts.title: Narrowing
concepts.summary: Control-flow analysis refines a union inside a branch from checks such as typeof x === 'string'.

concepts.title: Discriminated union
concepts.summary: A union whose members share a literal-typed property, such as kind, lets one check identify the member.

concepts.title: Exhaustiveness with never
concepts.summary: If every member is handled, the leftover type is never, and assigning it to never makes forgotten cases a compile error.

misconceptions: Learners think a union lets them use any member's properties. Only the shared ones are allowed until narrowed.
Learners narrow with a type annotation or as. A check on the value narrows it, and an assertion only silences the checker.
Learners rely on a default case. It hides new members, whereas a never check reports them.
sequence: function with x: string | number and a typeof branch.
A Shape union of circle, rect and tri with a switch on kind, and the error when tri is not handled.
A default branch with const _x: never = s.
An optional parameter name?: string and the possibly-undefined error.
examples: With type Shape = circle | rect | tri and a switch handling only circle and rect inside a function declared to return number, tsc reports TS2366: Function lacks ending return statement and return type does not include 'undefined'.
Adding default: const _x: never = s; reports TS2322: Type '{ kind: "tri"; b: number; h: number; }' is not assignable to type 'never'.
function greet(name?: string){ return name.toUpperCase(); } reports TS18048: 'name' is possibly 'undefined'; name?.toUpperCase() fixes it.

figures.shows: A union drawn as three coloured tiles with a branch tree; after each check the surviving tiles stay lit. Views: typeof check, kind check, never check.
figures.learnerAction: Click a check to see which members survive.

figures.shows: Code snippets with the cursor inside different branches and a choice of narrowed type.
figures.learnerAction: Pick the type at the cursor.

questionPlan.sample: Shape is circle | rect | tri. A function handles circle and rect in a switch and returns number. Which error code does tsc report for the function?

function greet(name?: string) { return name.toUpperCase(); }
Which fix handles a missing name at run time without a crash?

lessons.title: Generics
lessons.objective: Read a generic signature, predict the type argument TypeScript infers, and constrain a type parameter so only valid arguments are accepted.

concepts.title: Type parameter
concepts.summary: A placeholder such as T that the compiler fills in from the call, so one function can relate its input and output types.

concepts.title: Inference from the call
concepts.summary: The type argument is usually inferred from the arguments, and written explicitly only when inference cannot decide.

concepts.title: Constraint
concepts.summary: T extends Shape limits the argument to types with that shape, and lets the body use those members.

concepts.title: Generic containers
concepts.summary: Array<T>, Promise<T> and Map<K, V> are ordinary types that carry other types.

misconceptions: Learners think generics are just any. any loses the relationship between input and output, while T keeps it.
Learners think the type parameter exists at run time. It is erased with every other type.
Learners over-constrain or over-annotate. Let the call decide, and add extends only when the body needs members.
sequence: function first<T>(xs: T[]): T | undefined and the types of first([1, 2]) and first([]).
function longest<T extends { length: number }>(a: T, b: T) and why longest(1, 2) fails.
async function load(): Promise<number> and the type of await load().
id<T>(x: T): T with id(5) giving the literal type 5.
examples: first([1, 2]) has type number | undefined; first([]) has type undefined; first(['a', 1]) has type string | number | undefined (TypeScript 5.6).
longest(1, 2) reports TS2345: Argument of type 'number' is not assignable to parameter of type '{ length: number; }'.
async function load(): Promise<number> returns Promise<number>, and await load() has type number.

figures.shows: A function box with an input pipe labelled T and an output pipe labelled T | undefined; calls with different arguments colour T in.
figures.learnerAction: Pick an argument and read the filled-in signature.

figures.shows: Calls (rows, different from the questions) against the inferred type argument and result type, hidden until chosen.
figures.learnerAction: Predict then reveal.

questionPlan.sample:
function longest<T extends { length: number }>(a: T, b: T) { return a.length >= b.length ? a : b; }
Which call is a compile error?

lessons.title: Transforming types
lessons.objective: Use keyof, indexed access and the common utility types to derive one type from another, and predict what each accepts.

concepts.title: keyof and typeof
concepts.summary: keyof T is the union of T's property names, and typeof x takes the type of a value.

concepts.title: Indexed access
concepts.summary: T['name'] is the type of that property, and typeof arr[number] is the element type of an array type.

concepts.title: Utility types
concepts.summary: Partial, Required, Readonly, Pick, Omit and Record build new object types from existing ones.

concepts.title: One source of truth
concepts.summary: Deriving types from a value or a base type keeps them from drifting apart.

misconceptions: Learners rewrite near-identical interfaces by hand. Derived types change when the base changes.
Learners think Partial deep-copies optionality. It makes top-level properties optional only.
Learners think Omit checks its keys. Omit<T, 'typo'> compiles, so Pick with keyof is safer when keys must exist.
sequence: Take type U = { id: number; name: string; email?: string } and apply Partial, Required, Pick and Omit.
keyof U and a variable of that type given 'phone'.
const Color = { Red: 'red', Blue: 'blue' } as const, then type Color = typeof Color[keyof typeof Color].
Record<'x' | 'y', number> needs both keys.
examples: With U = { id: number; name: string; email?: string }, Required<U> demands email and const b: Required<U> = { id: 1, name: "a" } reports TS2741: Property 'email' is missing.
const c: Pick<U, "id"> = { id: 1, name: "z" } reports TS2353 because name is not in the picked type; Omit<U, "id"> is { name: string; email?: string }.
const Color = { Red: "red", Blue: "blue" } as const; type Color = typeof Color[keyof typeof Color] is "red" | "blue", so const d: Color = "green" is an error.

figures.shows: A type-transformer board: a base interface, a transformer chosen from a list and the resulting property list with optional and readonly marks.
figures.learnerAction: Choose a transformer and read the result.

figures.learnerAction: Match the need to the type.

lessons.title: Types at the edges
lessons.objective: Explain why data from outside is untyped, choose unknown over any, and read assertions, noUncheckedIndexedAccess and satisfies correctly.

concepts.title: any and unknown
concepts.summary: any switches checking off for a value, while unknown accepts anything but demands narrowing before use.

concepts.title: Type assertion
concepts.summary: value as T tells the checker to trust you, adds no run-time check and is rejected only when the types cannot overlap.

concepts.title: Unchecked index access
concepts.summary: Without noUncheckedIndexedAccess, xs[0] has type number even when the array may be empty.

concepts.title: Validate at the boundary
concepts.summary: JSON.parse returns any, so input is parsed into unknown and checked by a guard or a schema library before it is typed.

misconceptions: Learners think JSON.parse returns the shape they expect. It returns any, so a wrong cast hides the bug until run time.
Learners use as to convert. It never converts a value; it only changes what the checker believes.
Learners think strict mode checks array bounds. Only noUncheckedIndexedAccess adds undefined to index reads.
sequence: const j = JSON.parse('{}'); j.anything.at.all compiles; replace with unknown and the same line fails.
'5' as number is rejected, '5' as unknown as number is accepted and still a string at run time.
xs[0] on number[] under default and under noUncheckedIndexedAccess.
satisfies: const cfg = { port: 3000 } satisfies { port: number | string } keeps port as number, but the annotation widens it.
examples: JSON.parse('{}') is typed any, so const n: number = j.anything.at.all compiles; with unknown it is TS18046.
const t = "5" as number reports TS2352 (neither type sufficiently overlaps); "5" as unknown as number compiles and the value is still the string "5".
With noUncheckedIndexedAccess, const xs: number[] = []; const x0 = xs[0]; has type number | undefined; without the flag it is number.

const cfg = { port: 3000, host: "x" } satisfies { port: number | string; host: string } keeps cfg.port as number, while const cfg2: { port: number | string } = { port: 3000 } gives cfg2.port the type string | number.

figures.shows: A boundary diagram: untyped data (network, file, JSON) crossing into typed code through a validator, with the 'as' shortcut drawn as a dashed bypass labelled 'no check'. Views: validated, asserted.
figures.learnerAction: Send a bad payload through each route and see where it fails.

figures.shows: A short list of expressions (rows, not the same as the questions) and the type with and without noUncheckedIndexedAccess.
figures.learnerAction: Predict both columns then reveal.

lessons.title: What Node is
lessons.objective: Describe what Node adds to the JavaScript engine, choose between ES modules and CommonJS, and read configuration from environment variables safely.

concepts.title: Runtime
concepts.summary: Node packages the V8 engine with libuv's event loop, file and network APIs and a module system, so JavaScript can run outside a browser.

concepts.title: ES modules and CommonJS
concepts.summary: import/export modules are the standard, require/module.exports is the older system, and package.json type or the file extension selects which one a file is.

concepts.title: Built-in modules
concepts.summary: Built-ins such as fs and http are imported with the node: prefix, which marks them as part of the runtime rather than a package.

concepts.title: process.env
concepts.summary: Environment variables arrive as strings or undefined, so numbers and booleans must be parsed.

misconceptions: Learners think Node and the browser share all globals. Node has no window or document, and the browser has no fs.
Learners think process.env values keep their type. Assigning 5 stores the string '5', and a missing variable is undefined.
Learners expect __dirname in every file. It exists in CommonJS only; in ESM use import.meta.dirname.
sequence: List what a browser gives JavaScript and what Node gives it instead.
A file with import and a package.json with type: module versus a .cjs file.
process.env.N = 5 then typeof process.env.N, and Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000).
import { readFile } from 'node:fs/promises'.
examples: process.env.N = 5; typeof process.env.N is 'string'; Number(process.env.NOPE ?? 3000) is 3000; Number(undefined) is NaN (Node 22).
In an ES module typeof __dirname is 'undefined' and typeof require is 'undefined'; in CommonJS they are 'string' and 'function'.
import.meta.dirname and import.meta.filename are available in ES modules from Node 20.11 and 21.2; the sandbox ran Node 22.

figures.shows: A layered diagram: your code, Node APIs (fs, http, timers), V8 and libuv, operating system. A second view swaps the Node layer for the browser's DOM and fetch.
figures.learnerAction: Toggle runtimes and see which APIs exist in each.

figures.shows: Two columns, CommonJS and ES modules, with rows for syntax, __dirname, top-level await and how Node chooses the format.
figures.learnerAction: Fill each cell by choosing.

lessons.title: The Node event loop
lessons.objective: Predict the order of synchronous code, process.nextTick, promises, timers and setImmediate, and explain why blocking the loop stalls everything.

concepts.title: One thread of JavaScript
concepts.summary: Your code runs on one thread, so any long synchronous task delays every other callback.

concepts.title: nextTick and promises
concepts.summary: process.nextTick callbacks run first after the current operation, then promise callbacks, and both run before the loop moves on.

concepts.title: Timers and setImmediate
concepts.summary: Inside an I/O callback setImmediate always runs before a zero-delay timer, while from the main module the order is not guaranteed.

concepts.title: Offloading work
concepts.summary: I/O is performed outside the JavaScript thread, and CPU-heavy work belongs in worker threads or another process.

misconceptions: Learners think async means parallel JavaScript. Callbacks still run one at a time on a single thread.
Learners expect setTimeout(0) before setImmediate always. From the main module the order depends on timing, and only inside I/O is it fixed.
Learners think a loop of await calls is non-blocking, then run a CPU-heavy loop on the main thread and freeze the server.
sequence: Sketch the loop phases: timers, I/O callbacks, poll, check (setImmediate), close.
A CommonJS file with sync, nextTick, promise, timeout and immediate logs.
The same four calls inside an fs.readFile callback.
A while loop that spins for a second and delays a timer.
When to choose a worker thread.
examples: In a CommonJS script, console.log('sync'); process.nextTick(...'tick'); Promise.resolve().then(...'promise') prints sync, tick, promise (Node 22).
Inside fs.readFile(__filename, cb), logging tick, promise, setImmediate and setTimeout 0 prints tick, promise, immediate, timeout in that order.
In an ES module the promise callback runs before the nextTick callback, because module evaluation itself runs inside a promise job (checked in Node 22).

figures.shows: The Node loop as a ring of phases (timers, poll, check, close) with side lanes for the nextTick queue and the promise queue and a step button. Views: main module, inside an I/O callback.
figures.learnerAction: Step and read what runs next.

figures.shows: Five log lines from a script with nextTick, promise, timeout and immediate to place in order.
figures.learnerAction: Drag into order before stepping.

questionPlan.sample: Inside an fs.readFile callback you call setTimeout(f, 0) and setImmediate(g). Which runs first?
A request handler hashes a 200 MB file with a long synchronous loop and other requests stall. What is the best fix?
questionPlan.answer: Move the work to a worker thread or a separate process.
choices: Move the work to a worker thread or a separate process.
Use setTimeout(0) inside the loop body.

lessons.title: Files, streams and buffers
lessons.objective: Count the bytes in a string under UTF-8, convert between hex, base64 and text, and say when a stream's write signals backpressure.

concepts.title: Buffer
concepts.summary: A Buffer is a fixed-size block of bytes, and text becomes bytes through an encoding such as UTF-8.

concepts.title: Characters versus bytes
concepts.summary: A string's length counts UTF-16 code units while its UTF-8 size counts bytes, and the two differ for non-ASCII text.

concepts.title: Stream
concepts.summary: A stream moves data in chunks, so a large file can be processed without holding all of it in memory.

concepts.title: Backpressure
concepts.summary: write() returns false when the internal buffer reaches the high-water mark, and the producer should wait for drain.

misconceptions: Learners think length is the byte size. 'héllo'.length is 5 while its UTF-8 size is 6.
Learners think readFile is fine for any file. It loads the whole file into memory, which breaks for large inputs.
Learners ignore the return value of write(). Ignoring it lets memory grow without limit when the consumer is slower.
sequence: Count bytes: 'hello' versus 'héllo', '€' and an emoji.
Convert 'hi' to hex and base64 and back.
Compare readFile of a 4 GB file with a read stream piped through a transform.
Writable with highWaterMark 10: write 5 bytes, 5 bytes, 1 byte and read each return value.
pipeline() from node:stream/promises handles errors and backpressure.
examples: Buffer.byteLength('héllo') is 6 while 'héllo'.length is 5; '€' has length 1 and 3 bytes; '😀' has length 2 and 4 bytes.
Buffer.from('hi').toString('hex') is '6869' and toString('base64') is 'aGk='; Buffer.from('aGk=', 'base64').toString() is 'hi'.
A Writable with highWaterMark 10 and a slow consumer returns true, false, false for writes of 5, 5 and 1 bytes. In Node 22 the default highWaterMark for byte streams is 65536.

figures.shows: A pipe diagram: file, read stream, transform, write stream, each with a fill gauge and a highWaterMark line. Views: fast consumer, slow consumer.
figures.learnerAction: Start the flow and watch the gauge reach the line and pause.

figures.shows: Strings (rows) with columns for length, UTF-8 bytes and hex, hidden until the learner enters an estimate; strings differ from the questions.
figures.learnerAction: Estimate then reveal.

What is printed?

lessons.title: Serving HTTP
lessons.objective: Read a Node HTTP handler and predict the status, headers and body it sends, including routing from req.url and what happens when a response is never ended.

concepts.title: Request and response objects
concepts.summary: A handler receives the request (method, url, headers, a body stream) and writes a status, headers and body to the response.

concepts.title: Routing
concepts.summary: A router chooses a handler from the method and path, and req.url includes the query string unless it is parsed with URL.

concepts.title: The response contract
concepts.summary: A handler must set a status, a content-type and end the response, or the client waits until it times out.

concepts.title: Reading a body
concepts.summary: A request body arrives as chunks of bytes, which are collected, decoded and parsed, and bad JSON should return 400.

misconceptions: Learners route on req.url directly. It contains the query string, so '/users/42?x=1' does not equal '/users/42'.
Learners think the status defaults to something helpful. It is 200 unless set, which makes a missing resource look like success.
Learners think a handler that returns finishes the response. The response ends only when res.end() runs.
sequence: Parse new URL('/users/42?x=1', 'http://localhost') and read pathname and searchParams.
Choose 404 for a missing user, 400 for malformed JSON, 405 with an Allow header for a wrong method, 201 for creation.
A handler that writes a header but never calls res.end().
Set Content-Type: application/json and send JSON.stringify output.
examples: new URL('/users/42?x=1','http://localhost').pathname is '/users/42' and its split('/') is ['', 'users', '42']; req.url split('/') leaves '42?x=1' as the last piece.
A POST that creates a user returns 201 and a Location header; malformed JSON returns 400; a user that does not exist returns 404; DELETE on a route that only allows GET returns 405.
res.statusCode is 200 until set.

figures.shows: A request-to-response diagram with a handler box in the middle, the raw request on the left and the response on the right, with a router table beneath. Views: happy path, missing end().

lessons.title: Errors and concurrency
lessons.objective: Predict how Promise.all, allSettled, race and forEach with async behave, and what an unhandled rejection does to a Node process.

concepts.title: Promise combinators
concepts.summary: Promise.all rejects on the first rejection, allSettled always reports every outcome, race settles with the first to settle and any with the first to fulfil.

concepts.title: Sequential and parallel awaits
concepts.summary: await in a for loop runs tasks one after another, while Promise.all over started promises runs them together.

concepts.title: Unhandled rejections
concepts.summary: Since Node 15 a rejection nobody handles terminates the process with a non-zero exit code by default.

concepts.title: Cancellation
concepts.summary: An AbortController signal passed to an API lets the caller cancel the work, which rejects with an AbortError.

misconceptions: Learners think forEach(async ...) waits for the callbacks. It ignores the returned promises, so code after it runs first.
Learners think try/catch around a missing await catches the error. The rejection escapes because the promise is not awaited.
Learners think Promise.all cancels the other tasks when one rejects. They keep running; only the result is lost.
sequence: Three promises, one rejecting: Promise.all and allSettled results.
Three tasks of 50 ms each awaited in a loop and with Promise.all.
[1,2,3].forEach(async n => { await null; out.push(n) }) and out.length straight afterwards.
Promise.reject(new Error('x')) at the top level and the exit code.
examples: Promise.all([Promise.resolve(1), Promise.reject(new Error('boom')), slow]) rejects with 'boom'; allSettled gives statuses fulfilled and rejected (checked in Node 22).
Three 50 ms timers awaited one after another take about 150 ms; started together under Promise.all they take about 50 ms.
node -e "Promise.reject(new Error('x'))" exits with code 1; with a process.on('unhandledRejection') handler it exits 0.

lessons.title: Packages, versions and tests
lessons.objective: Read a semver range and say which versions it accepts, explain what a lockfile fixes, and read a node:test file.

concepts.title: Semantic versioning
concepts.summary: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, where a major bump may break callers, a minor bump adds backwards-compatible features and a patch bump fixes bugs.

concepts.title: Range operators
concepts.summary: ^1.2.3 accepts 1.2.3 up to but not including 2.0.0, ~1.2.3 accepts up to but not including 1.3.0, and below 1.0.0 the caret is stricter.

concepts.title: Lockfile
concepts.summary: package-lock.json records the exact version of every dependency, and npm ci installs exactly that.

concepts.title: The built-in test runner
concepts.summary: node --test runs files that use node:test and node:assert, with describe/it blocks and strictEqual for comparisons.

misconceptions: Learners compare versions as strings or decimals. 1.10.0 is greater than 1.9.0 though '1.10.0' < '1.9.0' as text.
Learners think ^ means any newer version. It stops at the next major, and below 1.0.0 it stops at the next minor or patch.
Learners delete the lockfile to fix errors. It is what makes installs repeatable.
sequence: Check the range ^1.2.3 against 1.9.0, 2.0.0 and 1.2.3-beta.1.
Check ~1.2.3, ^0.2.3 and ^0.0.3 against the next candidate versions.
Bump 1.4.2 by minor, major and patch.
A node:test file with describe, it, assert.strictEqual and a deliberately failing case.
Run npm ci versus npm install.
examples: ^1.2.3 accepts 1.9.0 and rejects 2.0.0; ~1.2.3 accepts 1.2.9 and rejects 1.3.0; ^0.2.3 accepts 0.2.9 and rejects 0.3.0; ^0.0.3 rejects 0.0.4 (checked with the semver package).
^1.2.3 does not accept the prerelease 1.2.3-beta.1; the minor bump of 1.4.2 is 1.5.0 and the major bump is 2.0.0.
semver.gt('1.10.0','1.9.0') is true while the string comparison '1.10.0' > '1.9.0' is false.

lessons.title: A typed service
lessons.objective: Design a small HTTP service that parses its configuration and every request body into typed values, fails fast on bad input and shuts down cleanly.

concepts.title: Configuration at startup
concepts.summary: Read and validate environment variables once at startup, so a missing variable fails the process immediately instead of a request later.

concepts.title: Parse, don't assume
concepts.summary: Turn unknown input into a typed value in one place, returning a result or an error, so the rest of the code sees only valid data.

concepts.title: Graceful shutdown
concepts.summary: On SIGTERM stop accepting connections, finish in-flight requests, close resources and exit.

concepts.title: Logs and health
concepts.summary: Structured logs with a request id and a health endpoint make a service operable.

misconceptions: Learners validate inside each handler. Validation belongs at the boundary so every handler receives typed data.
Learners call process.exit() in the signal handler. That drops in-flight requests; server.close() lets them finish.
Learners cast req.body as User. The cast checks nothing, so a malformed body reaches the database.
sequence: A config module that returns a typed object or throws with every missing key.
A parseCreateUser(input: unknown) function returning { ok: true, value } or { ok: false, error }.
A discriminated Result type and a handler that narrows on ok.
The shutdown order: stop listening, wait for in-flight work, close the database, exit 0.
A node:test file that checks the parser with good and bad input.
examples: type Result<T> = { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: string } lets a handler narrow with if (!r.ok) return 400.
Shutdown order for a service with a database: server.close(), wait for in-flight requests, close the pool, exit 0.
Config read once: const port = Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000) and a check that Number.isInteger(port).
